examples.problem:
The polar curve $r=7$ and the ray $\theta=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$ intersect at the point $P,$ as shown above. What are the Cartesian coordinates of $P?$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14040587/assets/728f7aad12a4f127cc002bc38c46fa87ba70d6ecd79ef311a0154014b649a0ce.png)
examples.worked_solution:
The polar coordinates of $P$ are $(r, \theta) = \left(7, \dfrac{4\pi}{3}\right).$ We can convert the polar coordinates of $P$ to Cartesian coordinates, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =7\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{4\pi }{3}) \\  & =7\cdot (-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{7}{2} \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =7\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{4\pi }{3}) \\  & =7\cdot (-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{7\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $P$ are $\left(-\dfrac 72, -\dfrac{7\sqrt 3}2\right).$

Given that the ray above passes through the point with Cartesian coordinates $(-5,-5\sqrt{3}),$ find the polar equation of the ray. Assume that the polar angle is in the range $[0,2\pi ).$

{{field-1}}.
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we find the reference angle associated with the point:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{R} & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{y}{x}| \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{-5\sqrt{3}}{-5}| \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡\sqrt{3} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the ray lies in the third quadrant. So, we find the angle in the third quadrant that has a reference angle ${\theta }_{R}=\frac{\pi }{3},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & =\pi +{\theta }_{R} \\  & =\pi +\frac{\pi }{3} \\  & =\frac{4\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the polar equation of the ray is 

$$
\theta =\frac{4\pi }{3}.
$$
